claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Cu to the current HEA composition will increase its thermal conductivity.
The Cu addition will preserve structural integrity under typical plasma-facing reactor conditions.
The current HEA intermediate layers are optimized for mechanical strength and stability but have moderate thermal conductivity.
Such HEA intermediate layers are currently used between tungsten and CuCrZr in plasma-facing reactor components.
Temperatures of approximately 700–900°C, high mechanical loading, high thermal gradients, and neutron irradiation loads are representative operating conditions for the proposed intermediate layer.
Minor Cu doping may subtly modify the HEA microstructure through nanoprecipitation or enhanced phase connectivity.
A 1–2 at.% Cu addition will avoid detrimental phase transformations.
Small Cu additions can establish additional electron and phonon conduction pathways within the HEA.
Plasma arc additive manufacturing can help maintain mechanical integrity by limiting process-induced stresses and improving mechanical properties.
The Cu-doped alloy will have higher thermal conductivity than the undoped intermediate-layer baseline.
The Cu-doped alloy will show no significant loss of tensile strength, hardness, or structural stability relative to the undoped baseline.
The anticipated benefit is restricted to controlled Cu concentrations of approximately 1–2 at.%.
Cu concentrations above approximately 1–2 at.% may adversely affect phase stability or mechanical properties.
The result may depend on plasma arc manufacturing parameters and the exact alloy composition.
Long-term neutron irradiation and cyclic thermal loading may cause Cu segregation or precipitate formation.
